entries.name: Human
entries.caption: A human needs its people. Alone, it goes to them, and they take it in. With a phone, it picks the phone up. The phone is full of people, and almost none of them knows this human. The relief lasts a second, so it picks the phone up again. In an experiment, thinking about a favourite media figure lifted a bad mood as much as thinking about a friend did, and left the loneliness where it was.

entries.name: Human
entries.caption: A few dozen people live in a camp, and a human knows all of them. A crying baby is picked up by many hands, work shows what it did, and danger is over in minutes. Nights are dark. When someone dies, the whole camp mourns. Millions live in a city, and a human knows a few of them. A crying baby gets one parent, every time. Work rarely shows what it did, and danger is on the news all day. The lights stay on at night. When someone dies, a few people mourn.

entries.name: Human
entries.caption: Foragers keep each other level. Among the Hadza, more than 80% of the meat of a large animal left the hunter's household. Wealth gaps in forager groups are about as small as income gaps in Denmark. In the USA the wealth gap is more than three times as large, and the people at the top are nobody you know.

entries.caption: In 85% of 190 forager societies, parents and close kin picked the partner, from the few hundred people within reach. Among the Aka, the range of a lifetime holds about 700 people to get to know. On an app you pick alone, the pool has no end, and everyone in it is a stranger. Of US couples who met online, 89% had no link before. One woman in New York got 1,504 first messages in a month.

entries.caption: A human body is built to move through the day. Hadza adults spend about 3 h 40 min a day in light activity and 2 h 14 min in harder activity, 14 times the harder activity of adults in large US studies. They rest about as many hours as people in rich countries, and close to a third of that rest is squatting or kneeling, which keeps the leg muscles working. A chair asks nothing of the body for hours.

entries.name: Human
entries.caption: Humans calm each other by touch, and it takes someone close. Under threat of an electric shock, a partner's hand lowered the brain's response to the threat and a stranger's hand did nothing. Ten minutes of neck and shoulder massage from a partner lowered stress hormones more than kind words did. In cafés, pairs touched each other 110 times an hour in Paris and not once in London. A week can pass with no touch at all.
